However, airlines and other aviation customers buying SAF would receive any benefits associated with purchasing the fuel. 2.1.3.2 SAF Blending SAF coprocessed at existing petroleum refineries and certified as ASTM D1655 fuel at the refinery is distributed throughout the supply chain in a business-as-usual manner. SAF produced at a stand-alone facility or biofuels facility (several plants also produce renewable diesel) require more consideration of where and when to blend with Jet A. Past studies have identified fuel terminals as the ideal location for blending due to fuel quality considerations (Moriarty and McCormick 2024; Moriarty et al. 2021). Terminals lease space for storage and blending activities to fuel producers, distributors, and marketers. Further considerations of where to blend SAF and Jet A include: • Fuel Terminals: Terminals are equipped with blending equipment, software, and staff, as they are currently designed to blend on-highway transportation fuels. The terminal could be directly connected to an airport via pipeline or may be thousands of miles away to address infrastructure constraints and the needs of fuel producers, suppliers, and end users. It is important to note that neat SAF from two different annexes (pathways) cannot be comingled into the same tank at the point of blending with Jet A (ASTM International 2025b; Energy Institute 2025). • Airports: Blending at an airport is not preferred for several reasons, including that it would be the first instance of certifying the SAF/Jet A blend as ASTM D1655 compliant; significant capital investment is required to add blending equipment, software, and additional off-spec tanks; impacts to airport tank farm insurance; increased truck traffic to airports for SAF delivery; and additional staff for blending operations. • Refineries: In limited instances it may be possible to deliver and blend SAF and Jet A in refinery storage. Refinery short-term storage is generally sized for the refinery capacity. A refinery would need offloading equipment to receive fuel by truck or barge/tanker. • Greenfield/brownfield sites: Establishing a new blending site near an airport or concentrated SAF production area is possible. Capital costs would be high, and permitting a new blending facility and associated pipelines would take years. This option would likely only be considered for geographic areas with significant capacity constraints for existing fuel infrastructure.
